contract: Socket.IO outgoing stream_progress: the transcode emits an immediate zero payload {stream, percent "0%", chunks [], numSegments 0} on start and, at each two-second segment check while the transcode runs, {stream, percent "<nn.nn>%", chunks, numSegments} with the created segments compressed into first-last ranges, to every socket of the owning user only.
exceptions: force is not applicable: the segment check runs on a fixed two-second timer; there is no force-refresh request.

The packet deliberately slows only its dedicated server's ffmpeg stand-in (FFMPEG_PATH wrapper that keeps the process alive) so the two-second check sees a running transcode with segments; the server itself is unmodified and the live upstream values are asserted.
The accepted playback lifecycle packet supplies scoped evidence and requires nonzero incremental progress per owner; its documented Go differences are deliberately not asserted here.

invariants.contract: A transcoded book first emits stream_progress {stream: session id, percent "0%", chunks [], numSegments 0} and then, on the first segment check that finds segments, {percent "100.00%", chunks ["0-10"], numSegments 11} (a chunk is the number of a single created segment and a "first-last" string for a run, as PlayerUi.setChunksReady handles both) on both sockets of the owning user and on no admin or other-user socket; a missing produced segment splits the chunk list into two ranges (percent "90.91%", chunks ["0-4", "6-10"] for one missing segment of eleven); a transcode that completes before the first check emits only the zero payload and nothing after stream_open.
While the transcode runs each segment check repeats the identical stream_progress payload and the percent never decreases, so a client that missed an update catches up on the next one.
A stream that fails on its input emits the initial zero progress, then stream_error, and no segment progress afterwards.
